questions.q: A qubit in superposition is measured and the outcome is 0. What is the qubit's state immediately afterward?
options: Still a|0⟩+b|1⟩, unchanged, because measurement is non-destructive
Exactly |0⟩ — the superposition has collapsed to the measured outcome
A weaker superposition, mostly |0⟩ but with a small remaining |1⟩ component
A 50/50 mixture of |0⟩ and |1⟩
questions.explain: Collapse means the state snaps to exactly the measured basis state — not a weakened superposition, not an unchanged state, but precisely |0⟩ with no remaining |1⟩ component.

questions.q: If you measure a qubit and get outcome 0, then immediately measure it again with no gates applied in between, what result do you get?
options: 0 again, with certainty (probability 1)
1, with certainty
0 or 1, each with 50% probability, since measurement always re-randomizes
It depends on the original amplitudes a and b, not on the first measurement's outcome
questions.explain: After collapse, the qubit is in the definite state |0⟩. Measuring a definite basis state again gives that same outcome with certainty — the randomness was resolved at the first measurement and isn't repeated.

questions.q: Why is collapse described as irreversible and information-destroying?
options: Because measurement takes a long time to complete
Because once the qubit collapses to, say, |0⟩, the original amplitudes a and b are gone and cannot be recovered by any operation
Because collapse only happens with faulty quantum hardware
Because collapse only destroys information if the qubit was entangled
questions.explain: The rich amplitude information (magnitude and phase of both a and b) that defined the pre-measurement superposition is gone after collapse. There is no gate or procedure that reconstructs the original superposition from the collapsed state.

questions.q: How does collapse's irreversibility connect to the no-cloning theorem previewed for chapter 5?
options: They are unrelated; no-cloning is a purely separate result

If you could clone an unknown state before measuring, you could measure the copy and still retain the untouched original, effectively evading collapse's destructiveness — no-cloning closes off exactly that workaround
No-cloning only applies to classical bits, not qubits, so it has no connection to measurement
Collapse proves cloning is always possible, since you can clone the post-measurement state
questions.explain: If arbitrary states could be cloned, you could sidestep collapse's destructiveness by measuring a copy while keeping the original superposition intact. No-cloning rules this out, which is why the two restrictions are intuitively linked, as chapter 5 formalizes.

questions.q: Why can't you insert a mid-circuit measurement into a quantum algorithm just to 'check progress,' the way you might insert a print statement in classical code?
options: You can; it has no effect on the rest of the computation
Measuring mid-circuit collapses the qubit out of the superposition the earlier gates built, destroying the unused amplitude information the rest of the algorithm needed
Mid-circuit measurement is impossible on any quantum hardware
It only causes a problem if the qubit is entangled with another qubit
questions.explain: An unplanned mid-circuit measurement collapses the qubit to a definite classical outcome, destroying the superposition and any amplitude information not yet used — which is why algorithms are built to measure only once, at the end, to extract the final answer.
